cues.text: Welcome back.
Imagine a wheel turning about a fixed axle.
A dot near the rim travels farther than a dot near the centre during the same
turn.
Yet both dots turn through the same angle.
That distinction is the starting point of rotation.
We measure angular displacement in radians.
One radian means the arc length equals the radius.
So arc length equals radius times angular displacement, provided the angle is
in radians.
A point half a metre from the axle turns through two radians.
Its arc length is one metre.
Notice that this is distance along a circular arc, not the straight line
displacement between its endpoints.
Angular velocity tells us how quickly the angle changes.
We call it omega.
Tangential speed equals radius times omega.
If our wheel turns at four radians per second, the dot half a metre from the
axle moves at two metres per second.
What about a dot halfway to that rim?
Take a moment.
It has the same angular velocity, but half the tangential speed.
In JEE questions, always distinguish angular quantities from linear quantities,
and check which radius belongs to the point being discussed.
Why is a long wrench easier to turn than a short one?
The turning effect of a force depends not only on the force, but also on where
and how it acts.
That turning effect is torque.
For motion in a plane, the torque magnitude about a chosen axis is radius times
force times sine of the angle between them.
Here radius means the position vector from the axis to the point where the
force acts.
An equivalent method is force times the perpendicular distance from the axis to
the force's line of action.
That distance is the lever arm.
Push perpendicular to a wrench, twenty five centimetres from the bolt, with
twenty newtons.
Convert the length to zero point two five metres.
The torque is five newton metres.
Now push directly along the wrench toward the bolt.
Predict the torque before calculating.
It is zero, because the force's line of action passes through the axis.
Choose an anticlockwise positive sign, then add clockwise torques with a
negative sign.
Torque uses newton metres, but we do not call it energy in joules: torque
describes turning tendency, while work describes energy transfer.
Mass tells us how strongly an object resists a change in linear motion.
For rotation, we also need to know where that mass sits relative to the axis.
This is moment of inertia, represented by capital I.
For point particles, add each mass multiplied by the square of its
perpendicular distance from the axis.
A one kilogram point mass half a metre from the axis contributes zero point two
five kilogram metres squared.
Move it to one metre, and the contribution becomes one kilogram metre squared.
Doubling the distance has quadrupled the moment of inertia.
That squared distance is the reason mass near the rim matters so much.
For a thin ring about its central perpendicular axis, the moment of inertia is
mass times radius squared.
For a uniform solid disk about the equivalent axis, it is one half mass times
radius squared.
The disk has some mass closer to the centre, so its moment of inertia is
smaller for the same mass and radius.
These formulas are not interchangeable, and changing the axis changes the
answer.
Before using a formula in an exam, identify the shape, the mass distribution,
and the axis explicitly.
Now combine the ideas in a worked problem.
A uniform solid disk rotates about a fixed axle through its centre,
perpendicular to its face.
Its mass is two kilograms and its radius is half a metre.
A constant net torque of one newton metre acts on it.
It starts from rest.
Find its angular speed after three seconds.
First calculate the moment of inertia: one half times two times half squared
gives zero point two five kilogram metres squared.
For a rigid body rotating about a fixed axis, net torque about that axis equals
moment of inertia times angular acceleration.
Divide one by zero point two five.
The angular acceleration is four radians per second squared.
Constant angular acceleration means we can use the rotational version of our
straight line equations.
Final angular velocity equals initial angular velocity plus angular
acceleration times time.
Starting from rest gives twelve radians per second after three seconds.
The angle turned is one half alpha t squared, or eighteen radians.
Here is an energy check.
Rotational kinetic energy is one half I omega squared, giving eighteen joules.
Constant torque times angular displacement also gives eighteen joules of work.
Two approaches agree.
Remember: the torque supplied in this question is the net torque, after
including any opposing torques.
A wheel rolling along the ground does two things: its centre moves forward, and
the wheel rotates about its centre.
We must include both parts of the kinetic energy.
Translational energy is one half mass times centre speed squared.
Rotational energy is one half moment of inertia about the centre times angular
speed squared.
For rolling without slipping on a stationary surface, centre speed equals
radius times angular speed.
Do not apply that constraint to a wheel that is skidding.
Try a uniform solid disk of mass two kilograms and radius half a metre, rolling
without slipping at a centre speed of two metres per second.
Its angular speed is four radians per second.
Translational energy is four joules.
Its moment of inertia is zero point two five kilogram metres squared, so
rotational energy is two joules.
Total kinetic energy is six joules.
What changes for a thin ring with the same mass, radius, and centre speed?
Pause and compare the moments of inertia.
The ring has twice the rotational inertia, so its rotational energy is four
joules and its total is eight joules.
That does not mean it has a greater centre speed; the speeds were specified
equal.
Your final checklist is axis, torque, moment of inertia, and any rolling
constraint.
These are foundations; angular momentum, axis theorems, and more advanced
rolling problems need further study.
